transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-02-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Lin (Redwood AE); Priya Shah (Redwood SE); Alex Moran (Redwood CSM); Marcus Lee (Aurelia CTO); Sofia Gomez (Infra); Ravi Patel (Security); Diane Chu (ML Eng)

[00:00] Jamie: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — sizing review from last week's telemetry, autoscale policy recs, burst planning, and any security open items. Marcus, can you confirm we still see the same traffic profile?
[00:18] Marcus: Yeah, hi. We saw that our peak in staging was 420 reqs/minute last week, roughly 3.2k tokens per request on average when the summarization flows run. There's a shorter tail at night. We also saw a few spikes where concurrent requests hit 110 simultaneous sessions.
[00:34] Priya: Got it. Last time we estimated 3 x A100-equivalent nodes for steady state, with burst capacity up to 6 nodes for the hourly spikes assuming continuous batching and KV cache warm. That was using the 32k-context quantized model we tested.
[00:50] Sofia: Quick Q — in production we may see shorter sequences but more concurrency. So I want to validate: does the autoscaler look at concurrent requests or token throughput?
[01:06] Priya: Good question. Our autoscale policy can be token-based (tokens/sec) or queue-depth (concurrent sessions). For this workload I'd recommend a hybrid rule: scale on token throughput as primary, with an upper cap on concurrent sessions to avoid memory pressure. The default burst rule adds nodes when token/sec goes above threshold for >30s.
[01:25] Diane: How does KV cache affect node counts? If we get a lot of prefix reuse, can we reduce nodes?
[01:33] Priya: Yes, KV cache (sometimes in our notes shown as K-V cash in transcripts, sorry) can massively reduce compute per-token for conversations with reuse. For single-turn summarization there's less reuse, but for session-based chat you'll see big savings. Practically, in our bench, enabling prefix caching reduced effective throughput needs by ~25-40% depending on reuse.
[01:52] Marcus: The other concern is latency. Our product SLO is 95th < 350ms for short responses. With batching we can save cost but we might increase tail latency. Thoughts?
[02:06] Jamie: That's the classic tradeoff — batching lowers cost per token but increases latency. Priya, what's our recommendation for meeting Aurelia's SLO?
[02:14] Priya: For 95th<350ms we recommend conservative batching: small continuous batches (batch size 2-4) with a max hold time of 15ms, and prefer hot-model replicas (no cold start). Autoscaler min nodes should cover expected sustained token/sec for 95th, with burst nodes configured to spin up quickly (we use warm pool pre-warmed GPUs in Dedicated). If you need ultra-low tail, you can reserve dedicated hot capacity (i.e., larger min nodes) and rely less on burst.
[02:40] Ravi: On security — KMS integration, audit logs, and data residency. We need to know if keys ever leave our HSM and how audit logs are stored.
[02:49] Jamie: We keep customer keys in your KMS/HSM — Redwood Private supports customer-managed keys and we can integrate via your KMS (AWS KMS or external HSM). Audit logs are exportable and we can set retention per contract. I'll share the SOC2 encryption spec and our audit log export doc.
[03:05] Marcus: Also, during spikes we'd prefer predictable throttling behavior versus failing open to hosted fallbacks. Can Dedicated be pinned so requests don't fallback to hosted instances?
[03:17] Priya: Yes, Dedicated can be configured with strict routing policies — prefer Dedicated, and if capacity exhausted you can choose either queue with backpressure or fail-fast. We often recommend an autoscale buffer and burst pool to avoid failovers.
[03:29] Sofia: What's the warm pool idea? How fast does a burst node come online?
[03:34] Priya: Warm pools are pre-warmed VM/containers with model loaded to memory but not actively serving. They can be promoted to serving in ~20–45s depending on model size and quantization. If you need <20s, we recommend some baseline reserved nodes always hot.
[03:48] Diane: For our pilot, what's a reasonable min/max node suggestion?
[03:52] Priya: Based on your staging numbers: steady 3 nodes (A100-eq) as min, scale to max 8 for bursts if you anticipate spikes up to 110 concurrent sessions; set burst threshold at token/sec > 12k for 30s. With KV caching enabled you could reduce min to 2 in chat-heavy scenarios but keep max at 6-8. We'll put these in the spreadsheet.
[04:15] Marcus: Cost question — any back-of-envelope monthly for 3 steady + 5 average bursts?
[04:21] Jamie: I'll include a cost estimate in the sizing sheet. We showed a model last week; I'll refresh with current pricing and quantization profile.
[04:29] Marcus: Perfect. One other thing — can Redwood support preemption policies if spot-like instances used for burst to save cost?
[04:36] Priya: Yes, we support mixed pools — reserved for baseline and spot for burst, with automatic fallback to reserved nodes. But note preemption adds cold-start latency if a spot node is lost; that's where warm pools help.
[04:49] Ravi: For compliance, we need assurance on data persistence in logs and model caching. Any persistent customer data left on the GPU?
[04:56] Jamie: No customer data is persisted beyond KV cache TTL; cache is in-memory and cleared on restart. For Private deployments we can provide stronger guarantees and ephemeral mounts. We'll add an explicit statement in the security doc.
[05:08] Alex (CSM): I'll coordinate dates for the on-prem walkthrough with the network team. Priya, can you lead that?
[05:13] Priya: Sure, happy to. I'll schedule a 60-min network & private deployment deep dive for the week of Feb 23.
[05:20] Marcus: Good. Final check — benchmarks. We'll run a 1-hour burst test in staging hitting 100 concurrent sessions and send the logs. Any specific metrics to capture?
[05:29] Priya: Capture token/sec, 95th/99th latency, memory usage, and KV cache hit-rate. Also capture queue depth and any queued request TTL expirations. We'll provide the script to run the load.
[05:41] Diane: Are there any vendor lock risks if we move to Redwood Dedicated? We currently evaluate Anthropic and Bedrock for redundancy.
[05:46] Jamie: Our platform supports model catalog portability — you can pin model versions and we can run open models. We'll share a model compatibility matrix. Competitors like Anthropic/Bedrock were mentioned but for this POC the emphasis is on cost/latency predictability and private deployment.
[05:59] Matt (silence/false label): [crosstalk]
[06:02] Jamie: Alright, recap: Redwood to share dedicated sizing sheet and autoscale policy recs; customer to run burst benchmark and share logs; security to get KMS/HSM and audit docs; schedule private deployment walkthrough. Any objections?
[06:17] Marcus: No objections. Thanks all.

End of transcript.
